specPoints.text: understand how to use the pH scale, from 0–14, can be used to classify solutions as strongly acidic (0–3), weakly acidic (4–6), neutral (7), weakly alkaline (8–10) and strongly alkaline (11–14)
know that acids in aqueous solution are a source of hydrogen ions and alkalis in a aqueous solution are a source of hydroxide ions
know that alkalis can neutralise acids

primer.text: From Acids, Alkalis & Titrations you know the pH bands from strongly acidic to strongly alkaline. This note explains what creates those values in water: acids release hydrogen ions and alkalis release hydroxide ions. It then shows how the two ions meet and cancel to make water, the reaction called neutralisation.

lessons.title: Acids & alkalis
lessons.opening: Dissolve an acid in water and it releases hydrogen ions, H+, and it is these ions that make the solution acidic. Alkalis dissolved in water release hydroxide ions, OH-, which make the solution alkaline. The pH scale is a measure of how much hydrogen ion is present, which is why stronger acids sit lower on the scale.
keyPoints: Acids added to water form positively charged hydrogen ions, H+.
It is the hydrogen ions that give the solution its acidity.
Alkalis in water release hydroxide ions, OH-, which make the solution alkaline.
The pH scale measures the amount of hydrogen ions present in solution.
pH below 7 means acidic, above 7 means alkaline, and 7 is neutral.

low.restatement: Acids put hydrogen ions into water and alkalis put hydroxide ions in, and whichever ion is in charge decides the behaviour of the mixture. The pH reading simply reports how many hydrogen ions are swimming about, so more hydrogen ions means a lower pH, while plentiful hydroxide pushes the reading high instead.
low.analogy: Think of H+ ions as sourness tokens and OH- ions as smoothness tokens: the more sour tokens in the glass, the more sour the drink tastes and the lower the pH goes.
low.examPointer: Link ion to property in every answer: H+ gives acidity, OH- gives alkalinity, and pH reports the balance between them.

medium.restatement: In aqueous solution the acid's molecules have released hydrogen ions while the alkali has released hydroxide ions, and each ion type defines the acidity or alkalinity of the mixture. Because the pH scale measures the hydrogen ion amount, a concentrated strong acid reads low while an alkaline solution with plentiful hydroxide reads high.
medium.analogy: Picture a scoreboard where hydrogen ions score for the acid side and hydroxide ions score for the alkali side; pH is simply the running total displayed.
medium.examPointer: Definition questions often quote the spec wording: acids are a source of hydrogen ions and alkalis a source of hydroxide ions, both in aqueous solution.

check.stem: Which ions do acids form when dissolved in water?

options.explanation: Acids in aqueous solution are a source of hydrogen ions, and these make the solution acidic.
Hydroxide ions come from alkalis, not acids.
Oxide ions appear in molten electrolysis chemistry, not in aqueous acids.

options.text: No ions form until the water is heated
options.explanation: Dissolving releases the ions at room temperature; heating is not required.

check.stem: What do alkalis release when added to water?

options.explanation: Alkalis in aqueous solution are a source of hydroxide ions, which make the solution alkaline.
Hydrogen ions belong to acids; releasing them would make the water acidic.
Water is the solvent; the alkali adds hydroxide ions to it.
Free electrons belong to metal lattices; solutions carry ions instead.

check.stem: What does the pH scale actually measure?

options.text: The amount of hydrogen ions present in the solution
options.explanation: The note defines pH as a measure of the hydrogen ion amount, which is why acids read low.

options.text: How dangerous the solution is to touch
options.explanation: Hazard is not what pH reports; the ion concentration is.
Temperature is unrelated to the pH reading described here.

options.text: The total volume of liquid present
options.explanation: Volume has no part in the pH definition.

check.stem: Why does hydrochloric acid solution turn litmus red?

options.text: Because the dissolved acid releases hydrogen ions into the water
options.explanation: The released H+ ions make the solution acidic, and litmus signals acidity with red.

options.text: Because hydrochloric acid contains chloride ions
options.explanation: Chloride ions are spectators here; it is the hydrogen ions that set the acidity.

options.text: Because litmus reacts to the green colour of the solution
options.explanation: The solution is colourless; litmus responds to acidity, not to colour.
Pure water is neutral; the acid added to it supplies the hydrogen ions.

check.stem: A solution reads pH 13 on the scale. What does it contain plenty of?

options.text: Hydroxide ions, OH-, making it strongly alkaline
options.explanation: A high pH means plentiful hydroxide ions, and 11 to 14 is the strong alkali band.

options.text: Hydrogen ions, H+, making it strongly acidic
options.explanation: Plentiful hydrogen ions would push the reading towards 0, not 13.

options.text: Neither ion type, since 13 is neutral
options.explanation: Neutral is 7; 13 sits deep in the alkaline band.
Pure water reads pH 7; a reading of 13 requires dissolved alkali.

check.stem: State which ions an acid forms when it is added to water.
check.modelAnswer: Acids form positively charged hydrogen ions, H+, in water.

check.stem: Classify a solution of pH 13 and name the ion it carries in abundance.
check.modelAnswer: pH 13 is well above 7, so the solution is alkaline, and it carries plenty of hydroxide ions, OH-.

check.stem: Explain why all acidic solutions, whatever acid made them, share the same core chemistry.
check.modelAnswer: It is the hydrogen ions, H+, that give a solution its acidity: every acid releases H+ in water, so the shared H+ ions give all acidic solutions their common reactions.

check.stem: A student tests three liquids: lemon juice, distilled water and oven cleaner. Predict their order from lowest to highest pH, naming the dominant ion in each.
check.modelAnswer: Lemon juice is acidic, so it has the lowest pH (rich in H+ ions); distilled water is neutral at pH 7; oven cleaner is strongly alkaline, so it has the highest pH (rich in OH- ions).

lessons.title: Neutralisation
lessons.opening: Neutralisation happens when an acid reacts with an alkali: the hydrogen ions meet the hydroxide ions and combine to form water, H+ + OH- giving H2O. Not every reaction of an acid counts, though; a metal reacting with an acid makes a salt but no water, so it is not a neutralisation. Bases such as limestone and quicklime are added to soils to raise a low pH for crops.
keyPoints: Neutralisation is the name for an acid meeting an alkali in reaction.
Hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions combine, and the product is water.
The net ionic equation for all acid-base neutralisations is H+ + OH- giving H2O.
Metal plus acid makes a salt but no water, so it is not a neutralisation.
Soils are treated with bases such as limestone and quicklime to raise the pH.

low.restatement: In neutralisation the acid's hydrogen ions join the alkali's hydroxide ions and water forms, leaving the mixture close to pH 7 instead of acidic or alkaline. Metal-plus-acid reactions make salts but no water, so they are not neutralisations, and bases such as limestone are used to lift acidic soils toward neutral for the crops.
low.analogy: It is like one plus and one minus cancelling to zero: the two opposite ions meet, and a calm, neutral water molecule is what remains after they snap together.
low.examPointer: Quote the net ionic equation H+ + OH- giving H2O, keep the metal-plus-acid exception ready for trick questions, and name limestone as the field example.

medium.restatement: Neutralisation is the pairing of hydrogen ions with hydroxide ions to form water, expressed once and for all by the net ionic equation H+ + OH- giving H2O, which is why the product solution can end at pH 7. The definition needs water: a salt forming without water, as when a metal dissolves in acid, does not qualify, and farmers use base additions such as limestone to lift acidic soils toward neutral.
medium.analogy: Think of the ions as opposite puzzle pieces snapping together; once every plus finds a minus, only calm water molecules remain on the table.
medium.examPointer: Exams reward the boundary: state the equation, then explain why the metal reaction misses the definition because water never forms.

check.stem: What is produced when H+ ions meet OH- ions?

options.explanation: The hydrogen ion and hydroxide ion combine to give a water molecule, which is the heart of neutralisation.
Hydrogen gas forms with metals, not when the two ions combine.
Carbon dioxide belongs to carbonate reactions; no carbon is involved here.
A salt forms alongside the water in a full equation, but the ions themselves make water.
options.misconception: salt mistaken for the ionic product

check.stem: Which is the net ionic equation for every acid-base neutralisation?

options.explanation: This single line covers all such neutralisations and explains why the result can be neutral.
That re-forms an acid; neutralisation removes the ions into water.
That dissolves an alkali; it is not the neutralisation step.
That is the reverse direction, the splitting of water rather than its formation.

check.stem: Why is magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid not a neutralisation?

options.text: A salt forms but no water is made
options.explanation: The definition of neutralisation needs the water-forming ion pairing, which the metal reaction lacks.

options.text: Because magnesium is too unreactive to count
options.explanation: Magnesium reacts readily; the classification fails on the missing water, not on vigour.

options.text: Because no salt forms in the reaction
options.explanation: A salt does form; it is the absence of water that excludes the reaction.

options.text: Because the acid is not concentrated enough
options.explanation: Concentration plays no part in whether the reaction is called a neutralisation.

check.stem: What are the products when hydrochloric acid neutralises sodium hydroxide?

options.explanation: The ions swap to give the salt sodium chloride plus the water made from H+ and OH-.
Hydrogen gas belongs to metal-plus-acid reactions; neutralisation makes water.
Neither product appears in this reaction; the pair is salt and water.
Those are the reactants, not the products.

check.stem: Why do farmers add limestone or quicklime to fields?

options.text: The bases neutralise acidic soil, raising the pH for crops that dislike low values
options.explanation: Neutralisation in the field lifts the soil pH, since some crops cannot tolerate values below 7.

options.text: To make the soil more acidic for special plants
options.explanation: The additions are bases, so they raise pH rather than lower it.

options.text: To add metal salts as fertiliser
options.explanation: The purpose named is pH adjustment, not fertilising.

options.text: To kill all the organisms in the soil
options.explanation: Nothing in the treatment targets soil life; it corrects acidity.

check.stem: Give, in ionic form, the single change that happens in every acid-alkali neutralisation.
check.modelAnswer: H+ + OH- -> H2O: hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions combine to give water.

check.stem: Magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid makes a salt but no water. Does this reaction count as a neutralisation?
check.modelAnswer: No: although a salt forms, no water is produced, so the reaction does not fit the definition of a neutralisation.

check.stem: Explain why mixing hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide always ends in the same neutral product once the reaction is complete.
check.modelAnswer: Because neutralisation is the pairing of H+ with OH- to form water, H+ + OH- -> H2O; once every hydrogen ion has met a hydroxide ion, only neutral water (pH 7) and the dissolved sodium and chloride ions remain.

check.stem: A field's soil measures pH 5, but the crop to be planted cannot tolerate pH below 7. Name what the farmer should add and explain the effect on the soil.
check.modelAnswer: Add bases such as limestone or quicklime: they neutralise the acidic soil, raising the pH towards 7 so the crop can grow.

glossary.definition: The positively charged ion, H+, released by acids in water and responsible for acidity.
The negatively charged ion, OH-, released by alkalis in water and responsible for alkalinity.
The scale from 0 to 14 that reports the hydrogen ion amount in a solution.
A solution in which the solvent is water.
The reaction in which an acid's hydrogen ions meet an alkali's hydroxide ions to form water.
A substance that neutralises an acid, such as a metal oxide, hydroxide or carbonate.

workedExample.prompt: a) State the ions responsible for acidity and for alkalinity in aqueous solution. b) Write the net ionic equation for neutralisation and explain why the product mixture can reach pH 7. c) Explain why magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid is not a neutralisation.
steps: a) Acids are a source of hydrogen ions (H+) in aqueous solution; alkalis are a source of hydroxide ions (OH-).
b) H+ (aq) + OH- (aq) → H2O (l): the two ions combine into water, which has a pH of 7, so the neutralised mixture can end at pH 7.
c) Metal + acid gives a salt and hydrogen, but no water is formed, so the reaction does not fit the definition of neutralisation.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) H+ gives acidity; OH- gives alkalinity. b) H+ + OH- → H2O; water is pH 7. c) No water forms, so it is not a neutralisation.
